title: Training a coding model to paint watercolours with TRL and OpenEnv
gist: The author fully open-sourced a reproduction of a viral aesthetic-RL project that trains an LLM to write JavaScript watercolour-painting code via GRPO, showing that RL over subjective taste works but that reward quality (a curated human-rated reference pool judged against a general aesthetic model) drives real quality gains, while trainer/infrastructure configuration, not the reward design, was the actual blocker to getting the pipeline to learn at all.

insights.claim: The original viral video, posted by Surya Narreddi on August 23, of an LLM painting watercolours via JavaScript (using the p5.brush library) had over 1.5 million views at the time of writing, but the original project published no open training artifacts, motivating this fully-open reproduction.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: Illustrates how quickly an unreplicable viral AI demo creates demand for an open, reproducible version — a recurring pattern worth watching in the open-source AI ecosystem.

insights.claim: The technique restricts the model to write about 150 lines of JavaScript using only 10 of the p5.brush library's 47 available drawing methods; the author argues this restricted action space (rather than the model's raw capability) is what produces the distinctive handmade watercolour aesthetic.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: A generalizable design principle: constraining a generative model's action/tool space can be a more effective lever for controlling output style than prompting or scaling.

insights.claim: The author frames the appeal of the project as a reaction against generative AI image models that produce 'perfect, statistically average' pictures, situating the imperfect, human-editable, code-visible output within the lineage of early generative art (DeepDream 2015, Edmond de Belamy 2018, Mario Klingemann's neural-network portraits).
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: Frames a market/cultural signal: audiences may be tiring of the visually 'perfect but generic' output of mainstream image generators, creating appetite for tools that expose process and imperfection.

insights.claim: Unlike most current LLM RL work, which uses verifiable rewards (math with known answers, code that passes tests), this project uses RLHF-style learned-preference rewards for a domain with no correct answer: aesthetic taste.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: A concrete demonstration that RL-over-taste is viable now, relevant to any application (design, music, writing style) where 'correctness' isn't verifiable and must instead be learned from curated human preference.

insights.claim: The reward function combines four weighted terms: a gate (0.05, compiles and doesn't cheat), length (0.05, favors longer code), a pairwise judge (0.60, style comparison against a curated reference pool via Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Instruct), and HPSv3, an open 7B aesthetic-preference model (0.30).
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: A reusable, concrete multi-term reward architecture for aesthetic RL that other teams applying RL to subjective/creative domains could copy directly.

insights.claim: Two of the four reward terms are themselves models trained on human preference judgments, meaning the ostensibly objective reward signal is actually a proxy for one or several people's subjective taste, shifting the real engineering effort from hyperparameter tuning to curating the reference dataset that defines 'good.'
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: Key strategic insight for any team building aesthetic/creative RL systems: the bottleneck and defensible IP is the curated preference dataset, not the model architecture or training code.
insights.quote: Two of the four terms in the reward function are models. Both are proxies for someone's taste.

insights.claim: Three GRPO runs were trained with different weight splits between the two judge models: judge-led (pairwise judge 0.60/HPSv3 0.30, run to 110 steps), hps-led (0.30/0.60, 110 steps), and hps-only (0.00/0.90, stopped at 60 steps as a pipeline-validation run).
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: Sets up a controlled comparison isolating the effect of weighting personal curated taste (pairwise judge) vs a general pretrained aesthetic model (HPSv3) in the reward mix.

insights.claim: Mean group reward rose across training in all three runs: hps-only 0.58 to 0.71 (+0.13), judge-led 0.45 to 0.72 (+0.27), and hps-led 0.57 to 0.82 (+0.24), confirming that even the harder, more personalized judge-weighted objective still successfully learns.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that optimizing toward a narrow, curated personal-taste signal (not just a broad pretrained preference model) is learnable via RL, expanding the design space for personalized generative-AI products.

insights.claim: Heavier weighting toward the personal pairwise judge produces a lower starting reward and a slower, noisier climb; the judge-led run spent its first thirty steps nearly flat before it began improving.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: Quantifies a real cost/tradeoff of optimizing toward a narrower personalized taste signal versus a broadly pretrained preference model — relevant for anyone budgeting compute for personalization-heavy RL runs.
insights.locator: just one more yolo run section

themes.theme: Debugging: the reward wasn't the problem, the trainer was

insights.claim: Multiple experiments that changed the reward design (swapping the reference pool, removing renderer noise, disabling the pairwise judge) all produced flat learning curves; the actual fix that unlocked learning was unrelated to the reward and instead was the trainer/optimizer configuration.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: A generalizable ML debugging lesson: when RL training stalls, check optimizer/trainer hyperparameters before assuming the reward function or data is at fault.
insights.locator: just one more yolo run section

insights.claim: Four specific trainer configuration changes unlocked successful training: learning rate raised from 2e-5 to 5e-5, LR scheduler changed from linear to constant_with_warmup, scale_rewards changed from group to none (a single gate-rejection was shrinking every other advantage in the group), and LoRA target_modules changed from a hand-picked list to all-linear.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: A concrete, reusable checklist of GRPO/TRL trainer configuration pitfalls that any team fine-tuning with GRPO should check first when a run fails to learn.

insights.claim: The default LoRA target_modules list assumes a dense model architecture, but Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is a mixture-of-experts model whose projections are named differently, so the adapter was silently training only 10 of 40 layers until the target list was switched to 'all-linear'; the routed MoE expert tensors remain frozen even with all-linear.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: A specific, generalizable gotcha for anyone LoRA-fine-tuning mixture-of-experts models: default target-module lists silently under-train MoE architectures unless explicitly set to reach every linear layer.
insights.locator: just one more yolo run section

insights.claim: Infrastructure failures (render timeouts, an unresponsive scorer) were initially silently scored as 0.0 reward, identical to a genuinely bad painting, corrupting the training signal; this occurred in about 1.5% of rollouts on average and up to 5.2% in the worst run, until fixed by excluding failed rollouts from the group instead of scoring them zero.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: A subtle but important RL-infrastructure lesson: silent infra failures masquerading as bad reward signal can meaningfully corrupt training at scale (up to 5%+ of samples in one run) unless explicitly detected and excluded.

insights.claim: A bug was found and fixed upstream in OpenEnv: the client's persistent websocket stayed cached as healthy even after being closed by the remote end, silently failing every subsequent call; this cost two half-finished training runs before diagnosis, and the fix was submitted upstream.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: A real contribution back to open infrastructure (OpenEnv) discovered through this project, and a warning to other OpenEnv users about a stale-websocket failure mode.

insights.claim: Reward variance between training steps is partly explained by which four reference images the pairwise judge happened to sample that step, not just model quality; GRPO's within-group advantage computation is largely robust to this since a hard draw moves the whole group's reward together, but raw step-to-step reward curves can still be misread as quality regressions.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: A methodological caution for anyone reading RL training curves with a stochastic reference-based reward: apparent 'bad steps' may reflect harder evaluation draws rather than real capability drops.

insights.claim: In all three runs, the initial reward gain came almost entirely from eliminating very bad outputs (near-blank canvases scoring under 0.3) rather than improving the best outputs; in the judge-led run, sub-0.3 rollouts fell from 99 to 16 across the run's thirds, and from 37 to 4 in hps-led.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: Shows early RL gains in this setting come from reliability/failure-elimination, not genuine quality improvement — a pattern likely generalizable to other RL-over-generation tasks and worth checking before crediting a training run with 'quality' gains.

insights.claim: In the hps-only run, the model became more reliable but not more beautiful: the best painting per step improved only +0.034 across the entire run versus +0.155 for the median, because HPSv3 stopped rewarding additional pigment once it recognized basic flower structure (petals around a center and a stem).
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: Evidence that a standalone pretrained aesthetic-preference-model reward saturates at mediocrity rather than pushing genuine top-end quality — a limitation to weigh when choosing between a general preference model and a curated comparative reward.

insights.claim: Adding the pairwise judge (comparison against curated reference paintings) is what drives quality improvement at the top end: it contributed +0.12 to the group mean in judge-led and +0.16 in hps-led (versus only +0.03 in hps-only), and paint coverage roughly doubled in both judge runs (0.11 to 0.23, and 0.13 to 0.30) but barely moved in hps-only.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: Reference-based comparative reward outperforms a standalone scalar preference model for pushing peak output quality — an actionable design principle for anyone building creative-RL reward systems.

insights.claim: The model learned to ignore an explicit system-prompt instruction to paint 15-30 filled shapes because obeying it wasn't correlated with reward: actual mean shape count stayed at 7-9, and shape count barely correlated with reward across runs (+0.000, -0.14, +0.07).
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: A clean, concrete demonstration that RL-trained models optimize the actual reward signal over literal prompt instructions when the two diverge — a caution for anyone assuming prompt instructions will be followed just because they're in the system prompt during RL training.

insights.claim: Output diversity collapsed within each run over training, with median paintings converging to look like the same flower, because GRPO optimizes toward matching a single-subject reference pool; the author argues a more diverse reference pool would be required to produce more diverse output.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: Reveals a structural tradeoff in reference-pool-based RL: reward-pool composition determines both the ceiling on quality and the diversity of outputs, meaning diversity must be deliberately engineered into the pool, not assumed to emerge.

insights.claim: Quoting Jason Liu, the author frames the project's central lesson as 'AI shifted the bottleneck from making to noticing' — curating and rating the reference pool is now the scarce, high-value human labor in aesthetic RL pipelines, not the model training or generation infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: A strategic framing relevant across creative-AI applications: as generation becomes commoditized, curation/judgment of what counts as 'good' becomes the defensible value driver.
insights.quote: AI shifted the bottleneck from making to noticing.

insights.claim: A side experiment found that a 4B-parameter model could already produce valid sketches passing the training gate, suggesting the 35B model used in the main runs may be far larger than necessary for this task, and that further validation could cut compute cost by an order of magnitude.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: A potential large cost-reduction opportunity if a smaller model can match the 35B model's quality — worth tracking for anyone estimating the true compute cost of production aesthetic-RL systems.
insights.locator: what I would try next section

themes.theme: The economics and infra footprint of aesthetic RL

insights.claim: A full training run requires roughly 18 GPU-hours on one H200 for 60 steps and about 34 hours for 110 steps, and a single 8-rollout training step takes 15-18 minutes, of which 70-80% is spent rendering (a single headless-Chromium render takes 69-96 seconds against a 90-second deadline).
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: Rendering, not the language model's forward/backward pass, is the dominant cost bottleneck in this pipeline — anyone estimating the true cost of code-generates-visual RL should budget for rendering infrastructure, not just GPU-hours for the model.

insights.claim: Four separate paid or hosted services (the trainer, the HPSv3 scorer Space, the RL environment Space, and Inference Providers for the pairwise judge) must all stay healthy simultaneously for a training run to succeed; only the Hub and the trackio metrics dashboard persist afterward.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: Reproducing or productionizing this kind of multi-service aesthetic-RL pipeline carries meaningful ongoing infra-uptime risk and cost beyond raw compute — a practical consideration for teams evaluating build-vs-buy.

insights.claim: The author republished the entire pipeline end to end — reference pool dataset with source sketches, RL environment, training scripts, trained model adapters, per-rollout datasets, and training curves — running fully on Hugging Face infrastructure (Jobs, Spaces, Inference Providers), explicitly to fill the gap left by the original viral project, which had no open artifacts.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: A fully reproducible reference implementation lowers the barrier for other teams or researchers to independently verify, extend, or adapt this aesthetic-RL recipe to other domains.

insights.claim: The author identifies multi-step training, where the model sees its own rendered output during training (currently the model 'paints with its eyes closed,' receiving only a single scalar reward with no image feedback), as the most promising next experiment, based on the observation that the reference pool itself was built using models that improved over three rounds of vision-critic feedback.
insights.speaker: Sergio Paniego
insights.so_what: Identifies a concrete, evidence-backed next lever (closed-loop visual feedback during training) likely to meaningfully improve output quality beyond the current single-turn, feedback-free setup.
insights.locator: what I would try next section
